title: Financial Inclusion and Financial Literacy in the Philippines: Implications on Saving and Financial Product Ownership
venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Business Economics and Technology
tldr: Financial literacy significantly increases the likelihood of account ownership and financial service usage in the Philippines, with higher savings and greater use of banking channels.
problem_and_motivation: The Philippines faces low financial inclusion, with 71% of adults lacking savings and only 28% having formal financial accounts. Understanding the relationship between financial literacy and financial inclusion is critical for policy development.
approach: Used data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) 2019 Financial Inclusion Survey covering 11,265 households across the Philippines.
Applied the Heckman two-stage method to control for selection bias in survey respondents.
Tested three literacy dimensions: basic (numeracy and compound interest), advanced (inflation and risk diversification), and digital (internet and online payment security).
Controlled for demographic variables including age, gender, education, income, marital status, religion, and geographic location.
Examined both account ownership (savings or credit) and financial service usage (sending/receiving payments, insurance, investment, pension) as outcome variables.
findings: Basic literacy positively affects account ownership: numeracy increases likelihood by 11% and compound interest knowledge by 4%.
Inflation knowledge increases both the probability of account ownership by 2% and the amount saved by PHP 24,851.
Risk diversification knowledge increases account ownership by 16% and savings amount by PHP 32,842.
Internet security knowledge increases the probability of owning a financial account by 7%.
Account ownership probability ranges from 18.75% for those with no financial literacy to 82.19% for those with all three dimensions.
Only 39% of respondents demonstrated proficiency in any literacy component.
Rural residents, older individuals, those with income below PHP 20,000, and those with elementary education show lower probability of financial service usage.

Table 5: Savings amount increases from PHP 21,056 (no literacy) to PHP 80,684 (all three dimensions).

definitions.definition: The capacity to understand and effectively use basic and advanced financial concepts including numeracy, compound interest, inflation, risk diversification, and digital financial security.
Access to and usage of formal financial services and products including bank accounts, savings, credit, insurance, investments, and pensions.
Numeracy skills and understanding of compound interest calculations.
Understanding of inflation effects and risk diversification principles.
Knowledge of internet security and protection from online financial scams.
A statistical technique correcting for selection bias by first modeling participation probability and then the outcome variable.
The central bank of the Philippines responsible for financial regulation and financial inclusion policy.

topics.name: Financial Literacy and Education
topics.justification: Directly examines the impact of basic, advanced, and digital financial literacy on account ownership and financial service usage among Filipino households.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides empirical evidence using nationally representative data that financial literacy is a significant predictor of financial inclusion in the Philippines. It quantifies the marginal effects of specific literacy dimensions on account ownership and savings behavior, informing policy interventions for financial education programs targeting underserved populations including rural residents, low-income households, and the elderly.
directly_justifies: Basic numeracy and compound interest knowledge significantly increase the likelihood of holding formal financial accounts.
Risk diversification knowledge increases savings amounts by PHP 32,842 on average.
Digital financial literacy knowledge protects consumers from online financial scams and increases account ownership.
Targeted financial education programs can bridge the inclusion gap for rural, low-income, and elderly populations.
limits: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference about the direction of the relationship between literacy and inclusion.
Self-reported survey data may be subject to recall bias and social desirability bias.
The study does not account for the quality of financial products available to different demographic groups.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan of all topic domains was conducted. Domain 3 (Financial Literacy & Education) was selected as the primary match because the paper directly studies financial literacy dimensions and their impact on financial inclusion outcomes. No other topic domains apply, as the paper does not address spending behavior analysis, budgeting systems, or technical forecasting.

limitations: Cross-sectional data limits causal conclusions about the direction of influence between literacy and inclusion.
Self-reported literacy measures may overestimate actual financial knowledge.
Does not examine the quality or suitability of financial products offered to different demographic segments.
remember_this: Account ownership probability rises from 18.75% to 82.19% as financial literacy increases across all three dimensions.
Risk diversification knowledge increases savings by PHP 32,842, the largest literacy effect on savings amount.
Digital financial literacy (internet security knowledge) increases account ownership by 7%.
Rural location, old age, income below PHP 20,000, and elementary education reduce financial service usage probability.
